title: The Doctor
source: Tate Britain, London (public domain: Fildes died in 1927). Wikimedia Commons or Tate, PD-Art.
caption: His one-year-old son died on Christmas morning. 14 years later, he painted the doctor who stayed all night. #art #arthistory #painting #history #oilpainting
_verify: VERIFIED 2026-10-10 (Wikipedia 'The Doctor (painting)', Tate): painted and shown at the Royal Academy in 1891; commissioned by Henry Tate in 1890 for £3,000; Fildes' first son Philip died of typhoid on Christmas morning 1877, aged one; Fildes built a cottage interior in his studio based on Scottish fishermen's cottages; lamp + dawn light read as an all-night vigil; 1947 US stamp for the AMA centenary; 1949 AMA campaign 'Keep Politics Out of this Picture' against Truman's national health plan.

That the doctor who treated Philip inspired the figure is the usual telling (Dr Gustavus Murray); Wikipedia says the final face resembles Fildes himself. Slides say 'the doctor who stayed', keep it loose.
Whether the child survives is interpretation (dawn = hope). Slide 7 says 'many read it'.

slides.headline: His son died on Christmas morning. Years later, he painted this
London, 1877
slides.text: Painter Luke Fildes loses his first son, Philip, to typhoid. The boy was one year old.

slides.headline: The doctor stayed
slides.text: What Fildes never forgot was the doctor who kept watching over his child.

slides.headline: A sick child
slides.text: She sleeps on two chairs pushed together, in a poor fisherman's cottage.

slides.headline: The lamp is still burning
slides.text: He has been here all night. Medicine could do little then. What he gives is his attention.

slides.headline: The parents
slides.text: In the shadows, the mother hides her face. The father's hand rests on her shoulder.

slides.headline: Dawn
slides.text: Morning light comes through the window. Many read it as hope: the child made it through the night.

slides.headline: Built in his studio
slides.text: Fildes built a whole cottage room in his studio to get the light right. Henry Tate paid 3,000 pounds for it.

slides.headline: It outlived him
slides.text: In 1947 it became a US postage stamp. It is still one of the most famous images of medicine.
